reconcile.connective: Defenders read this as normal genealogical compression: Matthew telescopes generations elsewhere, so 'begat' can span Jehoiakim without denying his existence.

discrepancy.connective: A modern evangelical study note states the underlying genealogical fact without qualification: Josiah was Jehoiachin's grandfather, not his father, as Matthew's begat-chain implies.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Josiah was the grandfather of Jehoiachin.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States plainly the actual generational relationship (grandfather, not father) that produces the tension between Matthew 1:11's 'begat' and 1 Chronicles 3:15-16.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Jeconiah was Josiah's grandson, being the son of Jehoiakim, Josiah's second son (Ch1 3:15); but Jehoiakim might well be sunk in such a catalogue, being a mere puppet in the hands of the king of Egypt (Ch2 36:4).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Concedes the literal grandson relation, then supplies the specific harmonization for this tension: Jehoiakim is elided from the 'begat' chain as an insignificant puppet king, consistent with Matthew's known generation-skipping elsewhere in the same chapter.

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871), on Matthew 1:11
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treats this specific passage directly, conceding Jeconiah's grandson relation to Josiah and explaining the terse 'begat' as eliding the intervening generation (Jehoiakim), consistent with Matthew's known generation-skipping earlier in the same chapter. Used in preference to Haley because Haley's specific coverage of this passage could not be confirmed.
